Music program offers hope for people living with dementia

  • July 22, 2026
  • By Crusader Staff
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:27
Instaread

A Northwestern University program that blends live music, lifelong learning and social engagement is giving new hope for people living with dementia and their caregivers, while new research suggests the approach can improve mood, stimulate the brain and reduce the isolation often associated with cognitive decline.

Researchers from Northwestern University’s Music and Medicine Program (NMMP) recently published findings in the journal Frontiers of Neurology showing that participants in the university’s innovative “Musical Museum” program experienced emotional, intellectual and social benefits after attending a series of concerts and educational lectures specifically designed for individuals with Alzheimer’s disease and related neurocognitive disorders.

The program was created in response to a challenge faced by many older adults with dementia. While research increasingly shows that lifelong learning may help slow cognitive decline, many people with dementia avoid traditional educational settings because they worry they will not be able to keep pace or feel embarrassed by changes in memory and language. The Musical Museum was developed to provide an enriching alternative in a supportive, welcoming environment where participants can enjoy music, learn something new and interact with others facing similar experiences.

Participants reported significant improvements in mood after attending the sessions, and many described the concerts as deeply meaningful.

One participant said the program “provided peace, relaxation and occasionally a cathartic release of tears.” Another praised the educational format, saying the historical background presented before each

performance helped deepen appreciation of both familiar and unfamiliar musical selections. Others highlighted the opportunity to connect with people experiencing similar challenges, describing the concerts as an important source of friendship and community.

Dr. Borna Bonakdarpour, director of the Northwestern Music and Medicine Program and the study’s corresponding author, said music remains remarkably resilient even as dementia progresses.

“Music stays intact for a long time for dementia patients, so the Musical Museum is a very good way for them to emotionally regulate and provide intellectual and cognitive stimulation,” Bonakdarpour said. “We always want to keep their brains engaged.”

Bonakdarpour, an associate professor of behavioral neurology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine and a Northwestern Medicine behavioral neurologist, developed the program with study co-author Clara Takarabe during the COVID-19 pandemic to continue providing meaningful enrichment opportunities for patients who had become increasingly isolated.

The Musical Museum now attracts an average of about 50 attendees per session. Each hourlong program combines live performances with discussions about the music’s historical, cultural and artistic significance. Organizers intentionally select a mix of familiar and unfamiliar works spanning genres such as jazz, bossa nova, baroque and other musical traditions.

Rather than simply presenting a concert, organizers structure each session around a broader theme, exploring ideas such as love, loss and the passage of time while connecting the music to periods that hold special meaning for many older adults, particularly the 1960s and 1970s.

Researchers say familiar music often comes from the period when participants were adolescents or young adults, a stage of life linked to powerful autobiographical memories. Previous research suggests these

familiar songs may help strengthen personal memories, reinforce self-awareness and reduce agitation among people living with dementia. Less familiar selections expose participants to new musical experiences while incorporating culturally diverse melodies and traditional folk influences from around the world.

Equally important are the receptions held after each performance, which encourage conversation among participants, caregivers and supporters.

Bonakdarpour said many people living with dementia withdraw from social activities because they fear making mistakes or becoming embarrassed as their language abilities decline.

“It’s common for individuals with dementia to isolate because they might feel nervous or embarrassed, especially if their language has declined, so this is a great way to get them out, and it’s a nice opportunity to see them outside the clinical setting,” he said.

The name “Musical Museum” reflects the philosophy behind the program.

“We decided to call it a museum because we treat each piece of music as if it’s something that’s curated for a museum,” Bonakdarpour said. “We merge science and creativity and provide a lifeline to those navigating the challenges of cognitive decline, creating joy and connection through art.”

Researchers say the program demonstrates that carefully designed arts-based experiences can serve as more than entertainment.
